## Linear Regression

### Simple Linear Regression

Linear regression aims to find the line of best fit for a given set of data points. Recall the method of least squares,
$$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\epsilon$$
where $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are the regression coefficients of slope and intercept, Y is our response variable, x is our independent variable, and $\epsilon$ is our error, which now in FHE, includes additional computation error. 

We assume a simple protocol where: 

1. Take as client input
$x=(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and $y=(y_1, \dots, y_n)$ 

2. Output a model $$\hat{y}=\hat{\beta_1}x+\hat{\beta_0}$$ that forms the line of best fit (slope and intercept) for our given client input and can additionally be input any new independent variable to generate predictions along the newly generated line.

These are immediate from our work: 

1. We can first compute $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ and
$\bar{y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$, which we can do since they are
**means**. 

2. We can compute the slope coefficient
$$ \hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$

3. The result is then easily
used to find the intercept $$\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}$$ using a multiplication and a
subtraction.

### (Sketch of) Multiple Linear Regression

**Multiple linear regression** extends the prior one-dimensional context
to allow for each data point to take multiple input features/
predictors. Recall the model for multiple linear regression: $$\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$$


A natural protocol is: 

1. Take as client input $$\mathbf{Y}=\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n\end{bmatrix},\space   \mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}1&x_{11}&x_{12}&\dots&x_{1k}\\1&x_{21}&x_{22}&\dots&x_{2k}\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&x_{n2}&\dots&x_{nk}\end{bmatrix}$$ where the $y_i$'s are the responses and each row of the $\mathbf{X}$ matrix is one observation's independent variables.


2. Output a model $$\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$$ that forms the line of best fit for our given client input and can additionally be input a set of new independent variables to generate predictions along the newly generated line.

Our desired weight
vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ can be computed with
$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{T}\mathbf{Y} $$  

The underlying parts, however, need more work. First, this approach
requires matrix operations, of which our explorations are very
preliminary (see [Dot Products and Matrix Multiplication](/other/matrix-multiplication.qmd)). Most crucially, the central difficulty
is that we would need to invert an $m \times m$ matrix; at a quick
glance, we can inherently approach this similarly to division using
Newton's method, as $$(I-M)^{-1} = I + M +M^2 + \cdots,$$ but there are
still many moving parts under the hood.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="**Remark**"}
See [^linear-regression-1] for some independent work on matrix inversion
under FHE.
:::

[^linear-regression-1]: Seunghu Kim, Seongbong Choi, Hyung Tae Lee;
